item.title: Special fijivillage Straight Talk Public Forum on Online Safety to be held at 7pm Friday September 4th
item.description: A special fijivillage Straight Talk Public Forum with Vijay Narayan will go live at 7pm Friday September 4th. The theme of the forum is Online Safety: Connected and Protected?
item.content:encoded:
A special fijivillage Straight Talk Public Forum with Vijay Narayan will go live at 7pm Friday September 4th.

The theme of the forum is Online Safety: Connected and Protected?

The panelists for the public forum will be Online Safety Commissioner, Filipe Barisal, Fiji Law Reform Commissioners David Solvalu and Valerie Narain.

The Straight Talk forum will focus on Online Safety Issues in Fiji, what is being faced by the Online Safety Commission, the feedback from the members of the public during the consultation process on the review of the Online Safety Act 2018, the call for age restrictions for Social Media, the response from victims, the changes being proposed and the reasons behind them amongst other issues.

You can also be part of the live audience by applying for registration with a question that you would like to ask during the forum.

The application to register details can be found on our website and facebook page, fijivillage.

You will receive a confirmation if you have been selected to be part of the live audience.

Please apply early to avoid any disappointment.

The show will be broadcast live at 7pm Friday September 4th on our Facebook, YouTube and X.

item.title: 7 chefs ready to fly Fiji’s flag at Melbourne Restaurant challenge
item.description: Seven of Fiji’s finest chefs are taking the flavours, creativity and spirit of the islands to Melbourne, Australia, where they will compete against some of the region’s best in the Australian Culinary Federation Restaurant Challenge. The chefs representing Fiji are Warren Mave in the Global Pastry Chef Challenge, alongside Maurisio and Masi from Laucala Island.
item.content:encoded:
Seven of Fiji’s finest chefs are taking the flavours, creativity and spirit of the islands to Melbourne, Australia, where they will compete against some of the region’s best in the Australian Culinary Federation Restaurant Challenge.

The chefs representing Fiji are Warren Mave in the Global Pastry Chef Challenge, alongside Maurisio and Masi from Laucala Island.

Ifraaz Hussein and Frances Wakeham from Sheraton Resort and Spa will compete in Team Challenge Category One, while Isireli Chong from Wyndham Resort and Filipe Miramira from Yasawa Island Resort will compete in Team Challenge Category Two.

Speaking to fijivillage News, Fiji Chefs Team Manager Kelevi Lalawailevu says the team is looking incredibly sharp and focused, with the energy in camp at an all-time high.

He says months of rigorous training have brought the chefs to peak physical and mental readiness, with their coordination in the kitchen now finely tuned.

Lalawailevu says Warren Mave and his pastry team are completely focused on the Pacific Rim Final, while the kitchen duos are also carrying a quiet confidence into the competition.

He says the chefs know Fijian island flavours are world-class and are excited to show the international culinary community what Fiji can do.

Meanwhile, four Fijian representatives will also assist with the Worldchefs judging panel accompanying Team Fiji.

They include Sheraton Executive Chef Rakesh, Wyndham Executive Sous Chef, Fiji Culinary Director Faruk, and Fiji Chefs Association Vice-President Amar.

The Restaurant Challenge begins tomorrow, and will end on Thursday.

item.title: Diabetes Fiji audit finds Central Division health facilities lacked diabetic foot care equipment
item.description: An audit of health facilities in the Central Division has found that none of the facilities assessed were fully equipped to provide diabetic foot care. Speaking to fijivillage News during the Pacific Islands Health Research Symposium, Diabetes Fiji Foot Care Project Officer Peni Butucama says the audit was carried out to assess how prepared health facilities were to provide diabetic foot care loca
item.content:encoded:
An audit of health facilities in the Central Division has found that none of the facilities assessed were fully equipped to provide diabetic foot care.

Speaking to fijivillage News during the Pacific Islands Health Research Symposium, Diabetes Fiji Foot Care Project Officer Peni Butucama says the audit was carried out to assess how prepared health facilities were to provide diabetic foot care locally, including whether they had the necessary equipment and specialised tools.

Butucama says the lack of adequate equipment has been a major barrier to providing diabetic foot care closer to where patients live, with many patients having to travel to the Diabetes Centre in Suva, which is already crowded.

The Project Officer says the findings have since been addressed through support from Australian Aid, which funds the foot care training programme and has provided equipment to health facilities.

He says foot care toolkits and autoclaves have already been distributed to facilities in the Central Division.

The toolkits include specialised equipment such as tissue nippers, probes to measure wound depth, nail trimmers, callous scrapers and surgical scissors.

He says autoclaves have also been provided to sterilise equipment after use and prevent cross-contamination between patients.

Butucama says the audit highlights the importance of providing nurses with both training and the necessary equipment.

He says nurses are being trained to provide diabetic foot care at their respective facilities, but they need the appropriate equipment to apply their skills effectively.

Butucama says the Western Division has also recently received foot care toolkits, while autoclaves will be distributed once they are procured.

An audit of health facilities in the Western Division is expected to be carried out soon, while the foot care training programme is now being expanded to the Northern Division.

item.title: Children need emotional safety, not just material things – Naisele
item.description: A child may have a comfortable home, attend the best school and have everything they need, but this does not necessarily mean they feel loved and emotionally safe. This was highlighted by Substance Abuse Advisory Council Director Josua Naisele, who says children do not measure love by what their parents buy for them, but by how they feel when they are around their parents.
item.content:encoded:
A child may have a comfortable home, attend the best school and have everything they need, but this does not necessarily mean they feel loved and emotionally safe.

This was highlighted by Substance Abuse Advisory Council Director Josua Naisele, who says children do not measure love by what their parents buy for them, but by how they feel when they are around their parents.

Naisele says children grow up surrounded by the emotions created in their homes, whether it is happiness, arguments, sadness or respect.

He says parents should therefore focus not only on providing for their children’s material needs, but also on creating a positive and supportive environment at home.

Naisele says a child can have a big room, attend the best school and have many toys, but still not feel emotionally safe if they do not feel loved, respected and supported.

He further says that parents should create a home that children look forward to returning to after school because they know they will be welcomed, listened to and treated with respect.

Naisele adds that making children feel safe, loved and supported at home can help strengthen their emotional wellbeing.
